trip_plan.totalNote: Hike to a 6,500-ft bench camp on day one, climb Chablis Spire's 4-pitch East Face via the Burgundy Col side on day two, and hike out on day three.

days.title: Hike to the bench camp
days.objective: Establish camp on the 6,500-ft bench
days.note: Leave the trailhead at Milepost 166 early (around 6 am) and hike to the bench camp at 6,500 ft in 2-4 hours. Set up camp, rest, hydrate and prepare for the next day.

days.title: Climb the East Face of Chablis Spire
days.objective: Climb the 4-pitch route and return to camp
days.note: Make an early alpine start from camp toward Chablis Spire via Burgundy Col or the direct approach, 1.5-2 hours to the base. Climb the 4 pitches to the summit in 3-4 hours, descend with 2 rappels in 1-1.5 hours, and return to camp.

days.title: Pack out to the trailhead
days.objective: Return to the highway
days.note: Pack up and hike back down to the trailhead, 2-4 hours downhill.

It's frequently combined with Burgundy or Pernod Spire for a multi-summit Wine Spires trip (add a day), and strong parties do the whole thing car-to-car in a single long day once the approach is snow-free.

trip_plan.totalNote: Hike from SR 20 to the bench or Burgundy Col on day one, then traverse to Chianti's east face, climb Lichen Bouquet, and hike out on day two.

days.title: Hike to Burgundy Col
days.objective: Camp on the bench or at Burgundy Col
days.note: From the SR 20 pullout, drop about 300 ft to cross Early Winters Creek, then climb the climbers' trail to the 6,400-6,600 ft bench (standard low camp, with a spring) or on up loose gullies and a snow finger to Burgundy Col. days.title: Climb Lichen Bouquet and hike out
days.objective: Climb the route, regain the col and hike out
days.note: From the col, descend 200-300 ft and traverse beneath Burgundy Spire's east face to Chianti's east face, under an hour. Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. Descend toward the Burgundy-Chianti notch or rappel Rebel Yell with two 60 m ropes, regain the col, and hike out.

trip_plan.totalNote: Hike from SR 20 to the bench or Burgundy Col on day one, then reach the Burgundy-Chianti notch, climb the North Face, and hike out on day two.

days.title: Hike to the bench or Burgundy Col
days.objective: Camp on the bench or at Burgundy Col
days.note: Hike from the SR 20 pullout to the 6,400-6,600 ft bench, which has good camping and water, or push on to one of the two or three austere, exposed bivy sites at Burgundy Col, where year-round snow supplies water. It is 3-4 hours to the col.

days.title: Climb the North Face and hike out
days.objective: Climb the route, regain the col and hike out
days.note: Traverse from the col to the Burgundy-Chianti notch and climb the North Face directly to the summit. Reverse the route to the notch and the snow traverse back to the col, then descend the gully and trail to the highway.

trip_plan.totalNote: A demanding 2-day outing: bivy at the ~6,500 ft bench below the west face, then a long, sustained climbing day (8 pitches, 5.10+) with a full multi-rappel descent back to the car — roughly 12-13 hours car-to-car on summit day.

days.title: Approach to Burgundy Col bivy

days.note: From the Hwy 20 pullout, a climbers' trail crosses a creek and climbs steeply to a bench camp (~6,500 ft), then continues up talus/gully terrain to Burgundy Col. A handful of small bivy spots sit at the col with year-round snow for water.

days.title: Climb the South Face, summit, hike out

trip_plan.totalNote: Hike ~5 miles up Cedar Creek and a rough path to meadow camp at ~6,200 ft, then climb the 8-pitch route, rappel, and hike out the next day.

days.title: Hike to the Silver Horn meadows
days.objective: Camp in the meadows at ~6,200 ft
days.note: From the Cedar Creek Trailhead, hike about 5 miles up the Cedar Creek Trail. Leave the trail below the old burn and work up along the south-face drainage to camp in the meadows at about 6,200 ft.

days.title: Climb the route and hike out
days.objective: Climb the 8 pitches, rappel, and hike out
days.note: Climb the 8-pitch route and rappel the southeast side back to camp. Hike out via the Cedar Creek Trail.

camps_on_file.name: Meadows below the Silver Horn's south face

trip_plan.totalNote: Hike up Cedar Creek to the meadow camp below the Silver Horn, then climb The Chalice and hike out the next day.

days.title: Hike in to the Silver Horn meadows
days.objective: Camp in the meadows near 6,200 ft
days.note: Hike from the Cedar Creek Trailhead to camp in the meadows near 6,200 ft below Silver Horn's south face.

days.title: Climb The Chalice and hike out
days.objective: Summit the Silver Horn
days.note: Climb the 8-pitch route to the summit and rappel the southeast side. Then hike back out via the Cedar Creek Trail.

trip_plan.totalNote: A standard 2-day trip: overnight at Burgundy Col or the larch bench, then a long summit day (roughly 10-11 hours) that finishes with a full descent to the trailhead; very fit parties can do the whole route car-to-car in one long day.

days.title: Approach to high camp

days.note: From the trailhead, climb a steep forested trail through the larch bench and on to camp. Most parties camp at the more sheltered larch bench; pushing on to the windier Burgundy Col instead makes for a shorter summit day.

days.title: Climb Gato Negro

days.note: Make an alpine start and approach the base of the route from camp. Climb the 12 pitches (one fast party of four went camp-to-camp in 9.5 hours), then budget several hours for the slow, loose descent gully.

trip_plan.totalNote: A 2-day, ~23-mile round trip with ~4,200 ft total gain: an easy PCT backpack in to Snowy Lakes camp, then a long summit-and-hike-out day on Tower's loose SW gully. Strong parties sometimes push the whole thing car-to-car in one very long day instead.

days.title: Backpack in to Snowy Lakes camp
days.objective: Establish camp at Upper or Lower Snowy Lake
days.note: An easy, scenic backpack almost entirely on the Pacific Crest Trail from Rainy Pass, over Cutthroat Pass and Granite Pass, then a short side trip up into the Snowy Lakes basin to camp. Trail is well graded and mostly moderate grade; multiple trip reports clock this leg at roughly 5-6 hours with overnight packs.

days.title: Climb Tower Mountain, then hike out
days.objective: Summit via the SW gully system and pack out to the trailhead
days.note: Leave camp with a light day pack for the summit push: cross talus below the west face (can hold snow early season), pass the large cave feature on the climber's path, then work up the loose class 3 gully with a short class 4 slab/exposed step near the top. After returning to camp, break it down and reverse the PCT back…

camps_on_file.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
camps_on_file.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Partie…

camps_on_file.name: Snowy Lakes basin
camps_on_file.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed sp…

camps_on_file.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
camps_on_file.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is…

camps_on_file.name: Granite Pass
camps_on_file.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed travers…

trip_plan.totalNote: A committing 2-day trip: ~9.7 miles and ~2,800 ft of net gain, but with a long, mostly off-trail approach and 2 pitches of loose, sustained class 4-5.8 climbing — most parties bivy once near the ABP-Larrabee ridge rather than pushing it car-to-car.

days.title: Approach to high bivy
days.objective: Reach a bivy site near the ABP–Larrabee ridge / "3rd bowl"
days.note: From Twin Lakes trailhead (~5,200 ft), hike over Low Pass and High Pass, then drop and traverse cross-country toward the boulders and flat spots below the American Border Peak–Mt. Larrabee ridge. About 80% of this is off-trail on talus, scree, and heather; water can be scarce late season so carry enough to camp dry if …

days.title: Summit push and full descent to trailhead
days.objective: Climb the Southeast Face chimney to the summit, then descend all the way out
days.note: An early start gets the technical ground done while rock is cold and other parties haven't kicked rock down. From the bivy, gain the notch/col below the face, traverse in, and climb the 2-pitch chimney system (rated 5.4, though several parties found it stiffer and harder to protect, more like sustained 5.8 in spots). camps_on_file.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
camps_on_file.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twi…

camps_on_file.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
camps_on_file.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pac…

camps_on_file.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass l…

camps_on_file.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
camps_on_file.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward B…

camps_on_file.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
camps_on_file.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone r…

camps_on_file.name: Lower Anderson Lake
camps_on_file.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because Bacon Peak's approach runs directly above it. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge…

camps_on_file.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
camps_on_file.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades t…

camps_on_file.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
camps_on_file.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traver…

trip_plan.totalNote: Three days: a steep, brushy climbers' path to Upper Blum Lake, a day crossing the Hagan Glacier side to the summit, and the long descent back to the Baker River trail.

days.title: Blum Creek path to Upper Blum Lake
days.objective: Climb from the Baker River trail to the lakes
days.note: Leave the Baker River trail at Blum Creek and follow the faint, flagged climbers' path. It is brushy, then steep forest to about 4,500 ft, then a talus traverse near 4,900 ft to Lower Blum Lake and on to Upper Blum Lake. Stay on the path: the brush off it is very hard going. A winter party camped higher, at about 5,600…

days.title: Hagan Glacier side to the summit
days.objective: Climb Hagan and return to camp
days.note: Traverse from the lakes onto the Hagan Glacier side and work up to the high ground. One party dropped packs at a high pass and scrambled the last few hundred feet; a winter party reached the highest point by a bowl and a short, roughly 50-degree chute to the ridge. Published summit heights range from 6,960 to about 7,1…

days.title: Descend to the Baker River trail
days.objective: Hike out from Blum Lakes
days.note: Reverse the steep climbers' path down Blum Creek. One party took about 2.5 hours down the path from the lakes; another lost the path below about 4,000 ft and found it again near Blum Creek.

trip_plan.totalNote: A 3-day, ~19.5-mile round trip with roughly 6,600 ft of cumulative gain: two long cross-country travel days bracketing one long, steep summit day. A very fit party can compress it into two long days, but three is the standard, more enjoyable pace.

days.title: Approach to Diobsud Lakes camp
days.objective: Cross-country from the Anderson/Watson Lakes trailhead over the Mt. Watson saddle to a benched camp above Diobsud Lakes
days.note: Trail hiking gives way to off-trail travel at Watson Lakes; parties climb to the terminal moraine below Mt. Watson, cross the saddle into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, then drop to open benches above Diobsud Lakes to camp. Mostly heather and open slopes with some route-finding, no technical terrain.

days.title: Climb Hagan's south slopes
days.objective: Round-trip summit of Hagan Mountain (7,067 ft) from Diobsud Lakes camp
days.note: From camp, bushwhack north up steep forest past two cliffbands to open heather and grass on Hagan's south side, then climb a talus/scree couloir to the SW end of the Hagan crags. A short traverse near the Hagan Glacier's ice apron leads to slabs that are scrambled to the summit; reverse the same line back to camp. Smal…

days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Anderson/Watson Lakes trailhead
days.note: Reverse Day 1: climb back over the Mt. Watson saddle and descend on trail from Watson/Anderson Lakes to the trailhead.

camps_on_file.name: South Hagan bench
camps_on_file.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give …

camps_on_file.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
camps_on_file.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so …

camps_on_file.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
camps_on_file.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. It is not on the way to Blum or Hagan. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-val…

trip_plan.totalNote: A classic 2-day, 1-night trip: ~5-6 hrs up to the Ruth Glacier notch camp on day one, then a long ~12-13 hr day two that combines the Icy Peak summit push (Ruth-Icy saddle, Icy Glacier, 100-ft Class 4 summit gully) with breaking camp and hiking all the way out; very strong parties occasionally link it car-to-car in one long (15-20 hr) day instead.

days.title: Approach to Ruth Glacier notch camp
days.objective: Establish camp at the Ruth Glacier notch (~6,600 ft)
days.note: An easy, well-graded trail to Hannegan Pass gives way to a steeper, looser climbers' path up Ruth Arm and a short root/rock gully with scramble moves, then snow/glacier travel up the Ruth Glacier to a flat camp at the notch. Most parties take 5-6 hours with overnight packs and set up before evening.

days.title: Icy Peak summit push and hike out
days.objective: Climb Icy Peak via the Ruth-Icy col and Icy Glacier, then break camp and hike all the way out
days.note: Drop from camp to the Ruth-Icy saddle, cross the Icy Glacier to the notch below Icy's Northwest Spire, then scramble to the base of the summit gully and climb the 100-ft Class 4 gully to the top. After returning to camp (roughly 8-9 hours round trip), break down camp and hike the full way back out to the trailhead the …

camps_on_file.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
camps_on_file.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usual…

camps_on_file.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
camps_on_file.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirel…

camps_on_file.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
camps_on_file.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth l…

camps_on_file.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
camps_on_file.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge…
